title: Underwood (2014): True or False
instructions: Check what each number refers to and distinguish association, prediction, and causation. Use the article to choose True or False.

items.prompt: On 4 June 1947, more than 70,000 11-year-old children in Scotland took the same intelligence test.
items.explanation: The Scottish Mental Surveys were among the first efforts to measure intelligence across an entire national age cohort. The article describes Sheila McGowan and more than 70,000 other 11-year-olds taking the test that day.

items.prompt: The Scottish Mental Surveys were originally designed to identify genes responsible for dementia in old age.
items.explanation: The original aims were to count children then considered unable to benefit from schooling and to investigate fears that average intelligence was falling as professional families had fewer children. The later cognitive-aging research made new use of these historical records.

items.prompt: The roughly 160,000 people mentioned in the article were surviving participants in the follow-up study in 2014.
items.explanation: Roughly 160,000 children took the original surveys in 1932 and 1947. Financial constraints made it impractical to recontact all surviving members of that original population; the number does not describe enrollment in the later follow-up.

items.prompt: The later-life follow-up ultimately enrolled 1,641 participants from the two Lothian cohorts.
items.explanation: The researchers reached out to nearly 5,000 people in the Lothian region near Edinburgh. The two cohorts ultimately contributed 1,641 participants, who repeated the original intelligence assessment and completed additional tests.

items.prompt: The finding that age-11 scores predicted about 50% of the variance in IQ at age 77 means that half of every individual's intelligence was permanently fixed at age 11.
items.explanation: The 50% refers to the proportion of between-person variation in IQ at age 77 predicted by childhood scores. It is not a fixed share of each person's intelligence or a statement that individual cognitive development is predetermined.

items.prompt: The apparent cognitive benefit associated with modest alcohol consumption disappeared after childhood IQ was taken into account.
items.explanation: Deary initially observed an association between alcohol consumption and cognitive performance, but it dissolved after adjustment for childhood IQ. The article interprets this as a case in which those who drank more were already likely to have higher cognitive ability, rather than evidence that wine improved cognition.

items.prompt: Because associations involving diet and social activity disappeared in the analyses reported in the article, all lifestyle interventions can be considered ineffective.
items.explanation: Some associations disappeared after childhood intelligence was considered in the Lothian data. This does not directly test every possible intervention, and Greenwood explicitly cautions against concluding that later-life mental function is foreordained or cannot benefit from intervention.

items.prompt: The Lothian findings suggest that roughly 50% of the variation in later-life intelligence remains unaccounted for by childhood IQ.
items.explanation: Childhood IQ accounted for about half the variation. Nonsmoking, physical fitness, bilingualism, and more education were associated with slightly better later scores than childhood scores predicted, and the article also identifies other genetic and environmental factors as possible contributors.
items.source: Variation not accounted for by childhood IQ

items.prompt: Across repeated testing, memory and knowledge performance held up relatively well, while abstract problem-solving and abilities involving fast thinking and reaction times showed age-related declines.
items.explanation: Both cohorts performed relatively well on tasks such as remembering a short story and pronouncing words, possibly partly because they became familiar with the tests. Performance on abstract problem-solving, fast-thinking, and reaction-time tasks declined relative to earlier testing.

items.prompt: Because cohort averages declined, every participant's cognitive scores changed in the same direction and by the same amount.
items.explanation: Scores spread out as participants entered their 70s and 80s, with many people diverging substantially from the average. Deary emphasizes that the mean does not describe the full pattern of individual change.

items.prompt: Diffusion tensor imaging findings linked the integrity of white-matter connections to roughly 10% of the differences in general cognitive function among Lothian participants.
items.explanation: Diffusion tensor imaging tracks the movement of water molecules through white-matter tracts. The researchers used it to relate the integrity of neuronal connections to differences in cognitive function.

items.prompt: High cortisol levels had already been established as the sole cause of white-matter hyperintensities.
items.explanation: The article says the causes of hyperintensities were still poorly understood. It reports a close link with high cortisol levels, not proof that cortisol alone causes them.

items.prompt: A relatively thin cerebral cortex in old age does not necessarily mean that a person has lost a large amount of gray matter during aging.
items.explanation: People with a relatively thinner cortex in old age also had lower IQ scores in childhood. Karama interprets this as suggesting that some may have started with less gray matter; the finding does not establish how much tissue each person lost over time.

items.prompt: The water tank hypothesis allows favorable early-life environments, to some extent, as well as genes to contribute to cognitive reserve.
items.explanation: The metaphor proposes that a better-organized brain early in life provides more reserve to draw down during neurodegeneration. The account explicitly mentions good genes and, to some extent, a favorable early-life environment.

items.prompt: At the time described in the article, ENIGMA included 33 institutions in 70 countries.
items.explanation: The numbers are reversed. The article describes a consortium of 70 institutions in 33 countries, which the Lothian studies joined in 2009.
